To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the evolution of social utility can be divided into two regimes, (ii) in the first one, utility rises monotonically as a result of rising income, (iii) in the second one, the opposite is true and welfare falls, and (iv) the transition from one to the other is gradual and takes place over a period that is relatively long compared to the lifetime of an agent.
(i) the welfare dynamics in a model of endogenous growth can be non-monotonic, and (ii) this non-monotonicity is due to the presence of a social norm of status competition.

in an overlapping generations economy where agents are endowed with a finite lifetime, the evolution of welfare can be distinguished into two regimes: in the first, welfare increases with consumption, whereas in the second, welfare decreases as consumption is replaced by leisure.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the study of the dynamics of social welfare in a growing economy, where the consumption and leisure of individuals are determined by a combination of the usual utility-maximizing behaviour and status concerns.
the study of the evolution of social well-being in the context of economic development.
the study of the dynamics of social welfare and the role that status concerns play in the process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evolution of welfare in a growing economy is non-monotonic.
the welfare of the representative agent is non-monotonic in the process of economic growth.
welfare is non-monotonic in time.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
status concerns can have a significant negative impact on the welfare of a population.
the welfare of a society can increase, decrease and remain constant over time depending on the relative strength of the status motive and the income motive.
, as a result of the presence of status concerns in an endogenous growth model, social welfare is non-monotonic over time.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the context of an overlapping generations economy, status considerations can be an important source of non-monotonic welfare behaviour.
the evolution of social utility can exhibit non-monotonic patterns, and that this is a consequence of the interaction between the dynamics of consumption and the dynamics of effort.
the evolution of social well-being is not necessarily a monotonic process in the context of an endogenous growth model.
